title: Trimming sheep hooves
subtitle: Keeping feet level and clean as part of a regular flock health routine.
excerpt: Sheep hooves grow continuously and need trimming two to four times a year, depending on ground conditions. Feet kept on soft or wet ground grow faster and accumulate more mud. An untrimmed foot folds over, traps mud and moisture, and creates conditions for foot rot. Here is how to restrain the sheep, use the trimmers, and recognise when a foot needs veterinary attention.
sourceNotes: NADIS (National Animal Disease Information Service), Lameness in Sheep (2023). Moredun Research Institute, Foot Rot in Sheep. SAC Consulting, sheep foot-care guidance.

glossaryTerms.definition: A contagious bacterial infection of the hoof tissue caused by the interaction of Fusobacterium necrophorum and Dichelobacter nodosus. Produces a characteristic foul smell, severe lameness, and softening of the sole and heel.

Placing a sheep on its rump with its back against the handler's legs for shearing, hoof trimming, or examination. Sheep become passive in this position as it removes their ability to balance and bolt.

content.text: Sheep hoof trimming is a routine task that takes 5 to 10 minutes per animal once you can
confidently. The objective is a level, clean sole and a straight hoof wall. You are not trying to cut as much horn as possible; you are restoring the hoof to the correct shape.
Stand beside the sheep facing its head. Place one hand on the near side of the neck and tilt its head away from you.
Push the sheep's hindquarters against your leg and tip it back onto its rump by swinging its front end away from you. The sheep will sit back between your legs.
Lean the sheep's back against your legs with its rump on the ground. It will stop struggling once balanced in this position.
Pick up the near forefoot and clean mud and debris from between the claws with the point of the hoof trimmer.
Trim the outer wall of each claw first, cutting parallel to the soft sole. Remove folded or overgrown horn in small slices rather than one large cut.
Trim the inner wall to match. The sole should be flat and both claws level with each other when the foot is placed down.
If you see pink tissue, stop. You are close to the sensitive corium. Cutting into the corium causes bleeding and pain. A very slight pink blush is acceptable; red means stop immediately.
Smell the trimmings. A sweet, foul smell indicates foot rot. Record which animal, isolate it, and consult your vet about antibiotic treatment.
Clean your hoof trimmers between animals with a dilute disinfectant solution if
is present or suspected in your flock. Dichelobacter nodosus survives on trimming equipment and can spread the infection to healthy animals.
